butir.teks: The fourth duty, which is among the subtleties of the craft of teaching, is that he rebuke the learner for bad character by way of allusion as far as possible, not explicitly, and by way of mercy, not by way of reproach. For explicit statement tears the veil of awe, breeds boldness in rushing into opposition, and stirs up eagerness to persist, since the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), who is the guide of every teacher, said, "If people were forbidden to crush camel dung, they would crush it and say, 'We were not forbidden it except that there is something in it.'" (١) The story of Adam and Eve (peace be upon them) and what they were forbidden alerts you to this. The story is not told to you to be an evening's entertainment, but so that you take heed through it by way of lesson. Also, allusion inclines noble souls and keen minds to derive its meanings, which yields the joy of grasping its meaning, out of desire to know it, so that he may know that it is among the things that do not escape his perceptiveness.

The fifth duty: one who takes charge of some of the sciences should not make the sciences beyond his own seem ugly in the learner's mind, like the teacher of language, whose habit is to disparage the science of jurisprudence (fiqh).

And the teacher of jurisprudence (fiqh) habitually disparages the science of hadith and Qur'anic exegesis (tafsir), saying that it is pure transmission and hearing, the business of old women, in which reason has no role. And the teacher of theology (kalam) turns people away from jurisprudence and says, "That is mere branches, talk about the menstruation of women, so where is that compared with talk about the attributes of the Most Merciful?" These are blameworthy traits of teachers, which ought to be avoided. Rather, one who takes charge of a single science should widen for the learner the way of learning in others, and if he takes charge of several sciences, he should observe gradual progress in raising the learner from one level to another.

The sixth duty: that he limit the learner to the measure of his understanding, so that he does not cast to him what his mind does not reach, lest it repel him or confound his mind, following in that the master of mankind (peace and blessings be upon him), who said, "We, the company of prophets, are commanded to place people in their ranks and to speak to them according to the measure of their minds." (٢) So let him disclose the reality to him when he knows that he can grasp it on his own. And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "No one tells a people a report that their minds do not reach but it becomes a trial for some of them." And Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said, pointing to his chest, "Here there are many sciences, if only I could find those to carry them." And he spoke the truth (may Allah be pleased with him), for the hearts of the righteous are the graves of secrets.

So the scholar should not divulge everything he knows to everyone. This holds even where the learner understands it but is not fit to benefit from it; how much more with what he does not understand? Jesus (peace be upon him) said, "Do not hang jewels on the necks of swine, for wisdom is better than jewels, and whoever dislikes it is worse than swine." Therefore it was said: measure out to each servant by the measure of his mind and weigh for him on the scale of his understanding, so that you are safe from him and he benefits from you; otherwise denial occurs because of the difference in measure. Some of the scholars were asked about something and did not answer, and the questioner said, "Have you not heard the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) say, 'Whoever conceals beneficial knowledge will come on the Day of Resurrection bridled with a bridle of fire'?" (٣) He said,

"Take off the bridle and go; if someone comes who understands and I conceal it from him, let him bridle me." For Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 4:5⟧, drawing attention to the fact that guarding knowledge from one who corrupts and harms with it is more fitting. And the wrong of giving to one who does not deserve it is no less than the wrong of withholding from one who deserves it.
Shall I scatter pearls among grazing cattle ... so that it ends up stored away with the shepherd of sheep?
Because they have come to be ignorant of its worth ... so I will not end up putting it as a necklace on the dumb beasts.
If Allah, the Subtle, shows subtle kindness through His kindness ... and I come upon people fit for the sciences and for wisdom,
I spread it, benefiting others and gaining affection ... and if not, it remains stored with me and concealed.
Whoever grants knowledge to the ignorant has wasted it ... and whoever withholds it from those who deserve it has done wrong.

The seventh duty: the limited learner should be given the clear matter that suits him, and he should not be told that beyond this there is a subtlety which he is keeping in reserve from him, for that weakens his desire for the clear matter, disturbs his heart, and makes him imagine that he is being miserly with it toward him, since everyone thinks that he is fit for every subtle science.

For there is no one who is not satisfied with Allah, glorified and exalted is He, regarding the perfection of his mind, and the most severe of them in foolishness and the weakest in mind is the happiest of them with the perfection of his mind.

By this it is known that a layman who is bound by the restraint of the Law, in whose self the beliefs transmitted from the early generations (salaf) are firmly rooted, without anthropomorphism and without figurative interpretation, whose inner state is also good, and whose mind bears no more than that, should not have his belief disturbed; rather he should be left to his trade. For if the figurative interpretations of the apparent meanings were mentioned to him, the restraint of the commoners would come loose from him, and it would not be possible to bind him with the restraint of delving into such matters, so the barrier between him and acts of disobedience would be lifted from him and he would turn into a rebellious devil, destroying himself and others. Rather, one should not delve with the commoners into the realities of the subtle sciences; with them one limits oneself to teaching acts of worship and teaching trustworthiness in the trades they are engaged in, and fills their hearts with desire and fear regarding Paradise and the Fire, as the Qur'an spoke of them, and does not stir up a doubt for them, for perhaps the doubt will cling to his heart and it will be hard for him to resolve it, so he will be wretched and perish. In sum, the door of inquiry should not be opened for the commoners, for it would disrupt for them their trades, by which the creation subsists and the livelihood of the elite continues.

The eighth duty: that the teacher act upon his knowledge, so that his deed does not belie his word, for knowledge is perceived by insight and action is perceived by the eyes, and those who have eyes are more numerous.

So when action contradicts knowledge, right guidance is prevented. Anyone who takes something and tells people, "Do not take it, for it is a deadly poison," the people mock him for it and accuse him, and their eagerness for what they were forbidden grows, so they say, "Were it not the sweetest and most delightful of things, he would not reserve it for himself."

The likeness of the teacher who guides, with respect to those who seek guidance, is like the engraving to the clay and the shadow to the stick. How could clay be engraved with what has no engraving in it? And when would the shadow be straight while the stick is crooked? Therefore it was said on this matter:
Do not forbid a trait while doing the like of it yourself ... a great disgrace it is upon you if you do.

Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 2:44⟧ And therefore the burden of the scholar in his acts of disobedience is greater than the burden of the ignorant, since a great multitude of people stumble with his stumble and follow him.
And whoever establishes an evil practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts on it.

Therefore Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "Two men broke my back: a shameless scholar and an ignorant man who affects devotion. The ignorant man deceives people with his devotion, and the scholar deceives them with his shamelessness." And Allah knows best.
